one_line_reason: Multiple Cochrane systematic reviews give consistent, dose-specific evidence that oral Harpagophytum procumbens reduces chronic low back pain, while osteoarthritis evidence for the same herb is mixed to null.

selected.population: adults with acute, sub-acute, or chronic nonspecific low back pain (Cochrane systematic review, 10 RCTs)
selected.intervention: Harpagophytum procumbens (devil's claw), oral, standardized extract
selected.dose_as_stated: daily doses standardized to 50 mg or 100 mg harpagoside
selected.primary_outcome: pain and use of rescue medication
selected.why_selected: most specific, dosed finding in the shortlist: two high-quality trials showed strong short-term pain improvement, with one demonstrating relative equivalence to 12.5 mg/day rofecoxib.

selected.population: adults with chronic nonspecific low back pain (updated Cochrane systematic review, 14 RCTs, 2050 participants)
selected.why_selected: most recent (2016) Cochrane update reconfirming devil's claw reduces pain more than placebo, though evidence quality is only moderate at best.

selected.population: adults with osteoarthritis (systematic review update, 35 RCTs across 22 herbal medicinal products)
selected.why_selected: extends the evidence to a second major indication (osteoarthritis) that catalog devil's claw products are also marketed for, with a favorable finding, though the review itself calls the evidence 'limited.'

selected.population: adults with osteoarthritis (Brazilian systematic review/meta-analysis, 16 RCTs total, n=1741; 1 trial of H. procumbens)
selected.primary_outcome: pain, physical function, swelling, stiffness, quality of life
selected.why_selected: an important counterpoint from a more recent, methodologically explicit meta-analysis finding no difference from control for devil's claw specifically in osteoarthritis, contrasting with the more positive low-back-pain evidence.

blockers: Effective doses are standardized to harpagoside content (50-100 mg/day), so a catalog product would need to state harpagoside percentage/standardization to map correctly; many generic Devil's Claw products may list only root/extract weight without this standardization.

Evidence is strongest and most consistent for chronic low back pain, while the osteoarthritis evidence across reviews is mixed to null (favorable in one older review, no difference in a more recent, larger meta-analysis).
The reviews themselves note heterogeneous extract preparations and only low-to-moderate overall evidence quality.

handoff_pmids.note: Dedicated systematic review of Harpagophytum procumbens safety across 28 clinical trials; found adverse event incidence not higher than placebo in double-blind studies, with minor GI effects in ~3% of patients, but calls for more long-term safety data.

excluded_pmids.reason: General narrative review of many osteoarthritis nutraceuticals (devil's claw, vitamin D, boswellic acid, curcumin, etc.); lists devil's claw without reporting specific trial data.
Earlier (2014) Cochrane low-back-pain review largely superseded by the more complete/recent Cochrane reviews already selected (17202897 for dose specificity, 26630428 for the most recent update).
2006 Cochrane low-back-pain review, an earlier version whose findings are essentially duplicated by the selected 2007 review (17202897).

Broader review of anti-inflammatory plant food supplements; concludes devil's claw (like turmeric) merely 'warrants further investigation,' a weaker and more cautious framing than the dedicated reviews already selected.
Osteoarthritis nutraceuticals review finding only 'limited evidence' for devil's claw, weaker and less detailed than the OA reviews already selected.
A methodological re-analysis note about which pain-index sub-components change during Harpagophytum/Salix low-back-pain trials; not itself an efficacy finding.
Dedicated 'Natural Standard' evidence-based systematic review of Devil's Claw, but the abstract provided contains no actual results or effect data, only a description of the review's scope.
